habitat: Pairs or single birds along large, slow-flowing, well-forested rivers. It is strictly nocturnal, roosts in dense foliage, and fishes from a low perch, dropping feet first.
summary: An uncommon, localised resident. A very large owl with dark eyes, cinnamon underparts and rufous-brown upperparts. The head looks flat at rest. The juvenile is much paler. The call is a deep resonant oogh, answered by a higher ooh. The Kemp name Pel's Fishing Owl and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: Verreaux's Eagle-Owl is grey, with pink eyelids and finely barred underparts. Pel's Fishing Owl is rufous-brown above and cinnamon below.

head.pattern: In repose the head looks flat, with only a slight suggestion of ear tufts. When excited the head feathers are fluffed and the head looks rounded. The eyes are dark in the description and black on the identification line.

upperparts.pattern: Rufous on the identification line and rufous-brown in the description.

head.pattern: The juvenile is much paler than the adult.

viewNotes.note: Dark eyes and cinnamon underparts. The head looks flat at rest.
When flushed it flies a short distance. The upperwing colour is not given separately.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: A deep resonant 'oogh', the mate replying with a higher 'ooh'. It also gives hoots, grunts and screeches. A grade A Zambia file is named as an ostrich and was not used. The selected file is a grade A call from Gabon. No Kruger recording was found. The filename is XC1190285-Pels-1.wav.

research.note: Newman calls it an uncommon, localised resident. The page banner also says locally rare, but Avibase does not mark the Kruger occurrence rare or accidental, so all twelve months are listed. The upperparts are rufous and rufous-brown. A grade A file from Zambia is named as an ostrich and was not used. The grade A call is from Gabon. The Kemp code RB was left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^6=64 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 32–128.
